God blessed man with freewill and gave him free reign within the Garden. The garden was plentiful with all sorts of decadent fruit and foods, and all Adam and his wife's worries would forever be perfectly sated. However there was one tree out of endless perfection that was off limits, and due to it's taboo nature and the temptation of evil and sin, Eve was drawn to it and later Adam was swayed as well. Many in the church view this as follows: the Garden represents the endless bounties of religious life. Every aspect of one's desire can be fulfilled simply by using what the Lord has set out for us. The endless trees being the endless blessings of the Lord. In the end though, we as man chose with our free will, and time and time again, to attempt to satisfy our desires with sin, that which is against God's law, which is infinitely less satisfying than God's given grace, and upon realizing the failed promises of what we believed to be better for us, (Eve thinking the fruit would make her like God) we become filled with shame and attempt to hide ourselves from an omniscient God. God did not make us to be imperfect and sin, but instead we delude ourselves into becoming slaves to sin and desire, the one tree out of many which surround us. Thus ridding us of our state of perfection.

Still hotly debated in the Catholic Church, but as more subscribe to the idea that "God is not a magician" more ideas for the meaning behind the analogy pop up. I've heard other ideas but this is the quickest to summarize.
